questions.question: Astronomers call the band of distances around a star where a planet's surface could keep liquid water the star's habitable zone. A red dwarf is a star far dimmer and cooler than the Sun. Where does a red dwarf's habitable zone lie?
questions.answer: Much closer to it than Earth is to the Sun
choices: Much closer to it than Earth is to the Sun
About as far from it as Earth is from the Sun
Much farther from it than Earth is from the Sun
Nowhere, since so dim a star cannot warm a planet
questions.context: A dimmer star gives off less light and heat, so a planet must circle closer to it to stay warm enough for liquid water. The red dwarf TRAPPIST-1 has three planets in its habitable zone, and all three orbit far closer to it than Mercury does to the Sun. Earth sits inside the Sun's habitable zone, while Venus lies inside its inner edge.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade teaches the habitable or Goldilocks zone, the distance from a star where water stays liquid, and applies the idea to stars brighter or dimmer than the Sun.

questions.question: The Moon circles Earth, so it travels round the Sun at the same distance and gets about as much sunlight. Yet it has almost no air, and most water left on its sunlit surface soon escapes into space. Why can the Moon not hold on to air the way Earth does?
questions.answer: Its gravity is too weak to hold gas
choices: Its gravity is too weak to hold gas
Earth's gravity pulls its gas away
It has no ozone layer to seal air in
It spins too slowly to keep air
questions.context: Some molecules of any gas move fast enough to escape a weak pull, and a gas molecule needs only about 2.4 kilometres a second to escape the Moon, against about 11.2 for Earth. Over the ages any air the Moon had leaked away into space; only in the coldest craters near its poles, never lit by the Sun, can ice last. Being in the habitable zone is not enough: a world also needs gravity strong enough to keep its air.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade lessons on why Earth supports life explain that a world needs gravity strong enough to hold an atmosphere, which the small Moon lacks.

questions.question: Earth's average surface temperature is about 15 degrees Celsius. Some gases in its air, called greenhouse gases, slow the escape of heat from the ground into space. Suppose they all vanished while the Sun shone just as before. About what would Earth's average temperature become?
choices: About -60 degrees Celsius
About -18 degrees Celsius
About 5 degrees Celsius
About 14 degrees Celsius
questions.context: Without its greenhouse gases Earth would average about -18 degrees Celsius, some 33 degrees colder than today and well below the freezing point of water. These gases are only a small part of the air, yet this natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth mild enough for liquid water. About -60 degrees is the average on Mars.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade teaches that the greenhouse effect keeps Earth's temperatures mild enough for life, warming it by about 33 degrees.

questions.question: Rocks laid down in Earth's early days show that its air then held almost no free oxygen. Today oxygen makes up about a fifth of the air. Where did the air's first oxygen come from, billions of years ago?
questions.answer: Microbes in the sea that made food from sunlight
choices: Microbes in the sea that made food from sunlight
Forests of plants that spread out across the land
Volcanoes that breathed it out of the ground
Rocks that slowly gave it off as they weathered
questions.context: Cyanobacteria, microbes in the sea that make their food by photosynthesis, gave off oxygen long before it gathered in the air: at first it joined with iron dissolved in the seawater, and only about 2.4 billion years ago did it begin to build up, in what is called the Great Oxidation Event. Plants first grew on land only about 470 million years ago, some two billion years later. Volcanic gas is mostly water vapour, carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide, not oxygen.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade lessons on Earth's atmosphere teach that its first oxygen was made by photosynthesising microbes in the sea, long before plants grew on land.

questions.question: Most of Earth's ozone gas lies in a layer of the air about 15 to 35 kilometres above the ground, in the stratosphere. Suppose the ozone layer above a town grew much thinner for a few months. What would the townspeople need to guard against more than before?
questions.answer: Sunburn from the Sun's ultraviolet light
choices: Sunburn from the Sun's ultraviolet light
Heatstroke from hotter air near the ground
Shortness of breath from air low in oxygen
Harm from the Sun's charged particles
questions.context: The ozone layer absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet light, which burns skin, harms eyes and can lead to skin cancer, so a thinner layer lets more of it reach the ground. The extra ultraviolet light does not make the air noticeably hotter, and the oxygen people breathe is in the lower air, not the ozone layer. Scientists reported a thin patch like this, the ozone hole, over Antarctica in 1985.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade teaches that the ozone layer protects living things by blocking much of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet light.

questions.question: Molten iron churning in Earth's outer core makes a magnetic field that reaches far out into space around the planet. Suppose the field vanished. What would then strike the top of Earth's air far more than before?
choices: The solar wind
Ultraviolet light
Infrared light
Bits of rock from space
questions.context: The solar wind is a thin stream of electrically charged particles, and a magnetic field pushes on moving charged particles, so Earth's field now steers most of them around the planet; a few are guided down near the poles, where they make the air glow as auroras. Light carries no charge and crosses the field unbent, and bits of rock from space are not steered by it either: the air itself burns most of them up as meteors. The ozone layer, lower in the air, is what holds back most harmful ultraviolet light.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade teaches that Earth's magnetic field shields it from the solar wind, one of the features that let Earth support life.

questions.question: A NASA spacecraft began orbiting Mars in 2014 to measure what the solar wind, the Sun's stream of charged particles, does to the planet. What did the spacecraft's team find the solar wind has done to Mars over the ages?
questions.answer: Stripped much of its air away into space
choices: Stripped much of its air away into space
Boiled its seas away with the Sun's heat
Blown its dust up into planet-wide storms
Turned its rocks and dust red with rust
questions.context: The solar wind knocks gas off the top of Mars's air into space, about 100 grams every second today and likely far more when the young Sun was stormier. In 2017 the spacecraft's team reported that most of Mars's air had been lost this way. Dry riverbeds show that water once flowed on Mars, which is now a frigid desert.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade compares Earth with Mars, a thin-aired, cold world that lost its magnetic shield and most of its air.

questions.question: Venus and Mars both have air made mostly of carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas. On Venus that gas warms the ground by hundreds of degrees, while on Mars it warms the ground hardly at all. What makes the difference?
questions.answer: Venus's air holds vastly more of the gas
choices: Venus's air holds vastly more of the gas
Venus's clouds let most of the sunlight through
Mars's carbon dioxide is too cold to trap heat
Venus spins so slowly that its long days bake it
questions.context: Venus's atmosphere is more than 10,000 times as massive as Mars's, so it absorbs far more of the heat rising from the ground; Mars has so little air that its greenhouse warming is slight. Venus's clouds actually reflect about three-quarters of the sunlight, and its nights are as hot as its days. Scientists call what happened to Venus a runaway greenhouse.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade compares Earth with Venus, far too hot, and Mars, too cold and thin-aired, to explain why Earth can support life.

questions.question: Volcanoes on Earth and on Venus have given off carbon dioxide for billions of years. On Venus nearly all of it has stayed in the air, which is now about 96 percent carbon dioxide. Earth's air holds only a trace of the gas. Where has most of Earth's carbon dioxide gone?
questions.answer: Locked up in rocks such as limestone
choices: Locked up in rocks such as limestone
Stored in the bodies of living things
Carried off into space by the solar wind
Frozen into the ice of the polar caps
questions.context: Rain dissolves carbon dioxide and slowly wears down rock, and rivers carry what it dissolves to the sea, where it settles as carbonate rock such as limestone. Earth's carbonate rocks hold about as much carbon dioxide as Venus's whole atmosphere. Venus has no liquid water, so its carbon dioxide stays in the air.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade compares Earth's air with Venus's and teaches that Earth stores much of its carbon in rocks such as limestone.

questions.question: Suppose an astronaut on Mars pours a cup of water onto the ground near the equator on a summer afternoon, when the ground there is warmer than 0 degrees Celsius. Why would the puddle soon be gone?
questions.answer: Mars's air is so thin that the water boils away
choices: Mars's air is so thin that the water boils away
Mars's gravity is so weak that the water floats off
Mars's days are so long that the Sun dries it up
Mars's winds are so strong that they blow it away
questions.context: The lower the air pressure, the lower the temperature at which water boils; even on a high mountain on Earth it boils below 100 degrees Celsius. Mars's air presses down with less than one percent of Earth's air pressure, so water there boils at about the temperature at which it freezes, and a puddle on warm ground boils away. A day on Mars is only a little longer than Earth's, its gravity, about 38 percent of Earth's, still holds water down, and its winds, in such thin air, push far more weakly than winds on Earth.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade compares Earth with Mars, a cold world with thin air and little liquid water, and explains why Mars's thin air will not let liquid water last on its surface.

Per the judge's fix the stem asks for the air's FIRST oxygen and a land-plant lure replaces the comets, so the student must know that microbes in the sea came some two billion years before plants on land. Fact-check uncertain: 'most' of today's oxygen overstated the microbes' share; asking for the first oxygen fixes it. The context's order is fixed too: the oxygen first joined dissolved iron, and only about 2.4 billion years ago began to build up in the air (F25, sourced now).
